speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43 relating to a crisis situation of the utmost concern to all Canadians. Canada's economic problems have become immense. This situation is too serious to be affected by the pressures of partisan politics. I would, therefore, hope that all members of this House will give careful consideration to the following motion. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan):
That it is the will of this House that the Prime Minister set up an all-party committee to deal with the very serious problems of inflation and unemployment, to draw up guidelines for wage settlements and arbitration rules to decrease the number and frequency of serious and crippling strikes and to study the recommendation of further immediate tax reductions to low and middle income Canadians.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED RECONSIDERATION OF ADMISSION FEE TO LOWER FORT GARRY-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to propose a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. I do so because in these days when Canadians are being urged to be interested in the heritage that is ours we in Manitoba find it difficult to understand the rather exorbitant fee that is to be levied, starting April 1, for admission to Lower Fort Garry on the Red River, in our province of Manitoba. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That this House urges the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to cancel the proposal, which has been set to come into effect on April 1, to charge a fee of $2 per person or $5 per family for admission to Lower Fort Garry, a place which should be open to all Canadians who wish to visit it, Lower Fort Garry being part of our western heritage and truly a national historic site.

speechtext: Has the government established any interdepartmental groups to examine the impact upon Canadian shipbuilding, ship repair and merchant seamen and officers of the possible ratification by Canada and sufficient others of the world community of the proposed Code of Conduct for liner conferences flowing from the UNCTAD meetings in 1974 and (a) if so, what is the membership and what are the terms of reference (b) if not, for what reason?

(b)	The Convention on a Code of Conduct for Liner Conferences has many optional provisions. For instance, the 40-40-20 cargo sharing formula would apply only when some other formula is not agreed. speechtext:
Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: 1. This inquiry appears to be related to the discovery of leaks in the pressure tubes of unit No. 3 of the Pickering generating station in August, 1974. The leaks in question are best described as internal leaks in that they involved leakage of heavy water from the pressure tubes (in which uranium fuel bundles are located) into a closed annulus formed by the pressure tubes and surrounding calandria tubes. There was no escape of this heavy water outside of reactor systems. Further barriers to the escape of such heavy water exist including the concrete reactor containment building. Extensive investigations by the owner, Ontario Hydro, and by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited have revealed the cause of the leaks and the necessary corrective measures including the replacement of a number of pressure tubes have been completed. It is expected that the unit will be returned to operation shortly.

Why was the Prime Minister not informed of this investi-

gation and the charges? speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not fair to say that the matter brought up by Mr. Kerr was ignored. It is quite apparent from the record that he made some allegations verbally, as he said, when he was mad. At that point the officials asked him to put the allegations in writing. Some weeks or a month or so later, I believe he proceeded to put the allegations in writing. The government acted upon those allegations. Investigation was followed through by the RCMP. Whatever evidence they gathered was given to the attorney general of Nova Scotia. At that point it was no longer in the hands of the federal government. There was no need to inform me of something which had been proceeded with routinely and had proceeded well. In Mr. Kerr's own words, his assessment is as follows: "I have no fault to find whatsoever with the higher echelon of the government in the way they handled this case. There was no suggestion of foot dragging or cover up. They reacted in a very smart and fast way. In fact, they reacted admirably."

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR, DEPUTY DIRECTOR AND FOR ADMINISTRATION OF MEASURE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The motion that was read was as follows: The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) moves that amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-29, respecting Canadian business corporations, be now read the second time and concurred in. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR, DEPUTY DIRECTOR AND FOR ADMINISTRATION OF MEASURE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The reason I want to make some comments on this matter is that the House is faced with 27 amendments as they appear in Votes and Proceedings and in my view one should note that they were made and accepted in the other place. Bill C-29 was debated at some length on second reading in the House. It had extensive hearings and discussions in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and was reported back to the House.
Unfortunately, the report stage and third reading were galloped through the House as the result of a last minute change in the order of business. As I recall, this business had been scheduled for a Monday afternoon in the latter part of January. The committee, of which I am a member, was making a trip to Washington at the time so the business of the House was changed. Bill C-29 was then hurriedly brought in on a Monday afternoon, on which day my colleague the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) was not present-he had piloted the bill through committee-so the bill was passed in a great hurry, without any debate. The penalty comes now, and I must say to those who feel the Senate has no place that this is a clear indication that there is nothing quite so foolish or tyrannical as an intemperate majority, and any highly technical and voluminous bill of this kind requires a second look. Thank goodness our colleagues in the other place gave it that second look, because the bill is now much more workable.

March 24, 1975
Canadian Business Corporations Act
Hon. members opposite, frankly, may not have even cracked the covers of this bill. They do not know about the absolute liabilities which are imposed, with absolute penalties for even innocent acts on the part of directors of corporations. Where the act imposed absolute liability, certainly events took, place. Of course, it was readily apparent to anyone who had any idea of corporate law that the penalties were far too strigent, so the appropriate amendments have been put in. I think they are amendments which all reasonable men would accept. Now the penalties will come into play if a person commits an act without reasonable cause. I invite hon. members to look at the series of amendments wherein time and time again the phrase "without reasonable cause" is repeated. We will have an act which is much more flexible. After all, corporate law is the framework within which a great deal of the economic activity in the country must be carried on. It cannot be made so stringent, so rigid and so bureaucratically hounded that corporations will not come to register and operate under the federal act.
This act is in competition with ten provincial acts, and it need not be said that a corporation has to incorporate under the federal Corporations Act in order to carry on business in any or all parts of Canada. Many provincial acts are very eminent and sensible pieces of legislation; they impose the appropriate degree of control to ensure that there is no dishonesty and that there is the required disclosure where necessary but not unnecessary disclosure.
There are many things required under this act in respect of which, as I told the predecessor of the present minister some years ago, neither the director of corporate affairs nor the minister himself were competent to collate the information obtained or even to interpret it. I remember the hosannas of some starry-eyed new members of this House who thought the bill was going to be the salvation of Canadian business and that this was to be a new charter. I am going back a few years. The funniest thing was that they did not know what they were trying to do, and when they tried to get the information they did not know how to interpret it.
There were a few woolly-minded academics who thought they might be able to get the information, but the act did not provide any means for collecting it; no one had the authority to collate it. Certainly the returns were there, as they are under the act as now amended. They may be examined for a fee, but who will go through the register of all the corporate files to collate this information? The director has not the authority, nor has the minister.
I would say that a good deal of what is alleged to be done under this act-that is, the justification for the reporting and the filing of returns-is empty windowdressing because it is done for no useful purpose. If I am interested in a competitor, I can send my solicitor or his clerk to have a look at the file and bring me the information. I can do that with regard to a number of competitors, whether federal or provincial, by having the appropriate searches made; but I cannot review the industry. I suppose I can, if I want to pay the money and if I know what to do with the information I obtain.
Years ago this was just empty window-dressing, and it still is, but the more rigid the requirements under the Canada Corporations Act, the fewer registrations there will be. This act is not a replacement for a national securities commission act. Somehow, in the bureaucracy of the minister's department, there is the idea that under this act the director of corporations can somehow carry out the role, in some unknown fashion, of the chairman of the Securities Commission of the province of Ontario or its counterparts in the other provinces of Canada. Somehow that idea has gotten abroad, but it is patent nonsense. There is no way this can be done, and I warn the minister or his parliamentary secretary who may be piloting this legislation that the more difficult this act is made, the fewer registrations will take place under it.
One does not have to register under the Canada Corporations Act in any way. I suppose it might be said that for some companies this would have to be done. I suppose if we wanted to start a new bank we would proceed under the letters patent provisions of this act rather than go through the gethsemane of having a private bill passed through parliament, the same as with a pipeline company-that is, an interprovincial pipeline company. Those are the only companies which perforce must come under this act, but an ordinary trading or manufacturing corporation can, frankly, cock a snoot at the director of Canadian corporations or the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR, DEPUTY DIRECTOR AND FOR ADMINISTRATION OF MEASURE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: They do now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR, DEPUTY DIRECTOR AND FOR ADMINISTRATION OF MEASURE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
As my colleague from Nova Scotia says, they do now, because provincial acts are more flexible and better for corporate activities: all that is required under the corporate act of a province is registration of incorporation, then an application for registry as a foreign company or extraprovincial company in another jurisdiction and one is in business without the nuisance of the Canada Corporations Act. I suggest-I have suggested this time and time again to the minister-that if he had wanted to do something really worth while for the benefit of the Canadian economy and the benefit of Canadian business, he should have those changes in the Canada Corporations Act which would have allowed corporations effectively to work and desire to be incorporated.
I do not know the percentage of Canadian companies operating under the federal act, but I venture to say that it is much less than 20 per cent of the total. It used to be something less. If it is more, it might be 21 per cent. That is wrong, Mr. Speaker; the reverse should apply. It seems to me that the nature of business in Canada today is that 50 per cent or 60 per cent of corporations and businesses could operate under a federal charter. It is easy to put "Ltd." behind a name. That can mean two truck drivers with two or three trucks, or a couple of plasterers. It does not have to be a huge multinational that operates as a corporation, yet an awful lot of nonsense is written about corporations and a good deal more is said about them.
I say to the government House leader that we will agree to these amendments having second reading as they are an improvement to the bill. I find it strange, however, that

March 24, 1975

the minister would schedule the bill for debate today when the record of proceedings in the other place, where these amendments were discussed, has not been published: the good and valuable work that was done by the hon. Senators who proposed the amendments, and the replies of the minister and his officers, are not available to us. For the government House leader to bring in the bill under these circumstances is sloppy practice. My colleagues and I would have appreciated the courtesy of a few hours to peruse the reasons for the amendments and the contribution of the minister. I do not want to carp on this, but it is part of what we should consider to be the intelligent operation of this House. I think the government House leader and his colleagues have blotted their copybook this afternoon.
Notwithstanding that, Mr. Speaker, having studied these amendments in detail I must say they are acceptable to the official opposition and I hope we can give them second reading. They are an improvement to the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR, DEPUTY DIRECTOR AND FOR ADMINISTRATION OF MEASURE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only want to make a couple of brief comments in response to the statements of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) with respect to rushing Bill C-29 through report stage and third reading in this chamber. I know the hon. member realizes that report stage is not subject to debate unless an amendment has been filed, which was not the case here. It is not the responsibility of the government to file amendments to its own legislation at report stage. As far as third reading is concerned, there was the opportunity for members to debate the bill at that time. Some hon. members may feel aggrieved by the length of notice given, but the action was completely in accordance with the rules and I believe was taken after discussion among all House leaders. I think the hon. member was not in the chamber at that time, for good and legitimate reasons, but his point is valid.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the amendments put forward in the other place are good, useful and worth-while. I believe they are a further indication of the kind of concern that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has brought to the consideration of Bill C-29 in response to representations made in this House and in the committee of the other place. As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, this clearly proves that the Senate has a valuable role to play in terms of having a second look at legislation. The government has no objection whatsoever to the amendments put forward by that body.
In response to the more substantive point made by the hon. member for Edmonton West regarding these specific amendments, I should like to deal with that as quickly as I can. Knowing that the bill has been in the public domain for a long time, the Senate committee worked hard and diligently to consider it in as short a time as possible. There was an extremely broad basis of agreement in the business community, and I think in this House, that it was fundamentally a good bill. The Senate analysed the bill very thoroughly and scrutinized the central issues carefully. They asked good questions and suggested amendments only in respect of provisions they felt strongly about, and they gave full reasons for the amendments they put for-
Canadian Business Corporations Act ward. On the whole, the appearance before them was a pleasant and rewarding experience.
The Senate committee clearly approved the central goals of the bill, that is, to rid the law of useless formalities, to simplify administration, to clarify the substantive rules of corporation law and, in general, to achieve a fair balance between management and shareholders that gives managers broad powers but that, at the same time, furnishes remedies to shareholders in order to enable them to check any management abuses.
The specific amendments made by the Senate fall into three broad categories: first, changes of wording to clarify a technical error or ambiguity; second, substantive changes concerning close corporations, resident Canadian directors and investigations; third, amendments to the strict liability penal provisions to permit a defence of reasonable excuse for failure to comply with the law.
The first of the wording changes, which concerns item 6 of the schedule of the bill, is unanimously agreed by all concerned to be an essential technical amendment to clarify a drafting error in the present bill which would limit the National Energy Board's licensing powers to the granting of a licence only to a corporation already holding a licence, precluding a new corporation from obtaining a licence to operate a pipeline.
The other significant wording changes concern clause 4 which is amended to clarify a constitutional uncertainty implied by the present draft, and also clauses 180, 181 and 182 which are amended to make certain that in case of amalgamation or continuance an individual who first becomes a director or officer of a corporation after an amalgamation or continuance is not personally liable for acts of directors and officers of a pertinent corporation before the amalgamation or continuance.
In its second group of amendments, the Senate modified clause 21 to increase the privacy of shareholders in closely-held corporations and amended clauses 110 and 116 to clarify the liability of directors in connection with the delegation of their functions to committees of directors and to officers. The Senate also amended clause 222 to ensure that an ex parte application for an investigation of a corporation must be conducted in private, to preclude any person from using this remedy as a device to secure groundless publicity.
Similarly, the Senate amended clauses 106(1) and 109(3) to empower the remaining directors of a corporation, even without the required Canadian majority, to fill a vacancy caused by the death or resignation of a Canadian director. The stated goal of the amendment is not to change existing policy or to water down the effectiveness of the Canadian director provisions but, rather, to make them work better by simplifying the process of maintaining a majority of Canadian directors on the board.
In the third group, the Senate amended several strict liability penal sanctions to permit an accused to establish that he has reasonable cause for not complying with the law. The department officials and I did not object strongly to these amendments, pointing out that the corporation law is not based on the criminal power, and therefore that the criminal sanctions serve only as a veiled threat to

March 24, 1975
Canadian Business Corporations Act
secure compliance, and that the bill relies mainly for its enforcement not on criminal sanctions but, instead, on effective civil and administrative remedies which make the corporation law as self-enforcing as possible.
The Senate committee studied the bill professionally, objectively and fairly, limiting their amendments to what they strongly felt were substantive improvements. We therefore agreed and I agreed on behalf of the government, to the changes recommended by the Senate committee that I have already outlined.
As I mentioned during the second reading debate in this chamber, the development process that has led up to today's debate on the Canada business corporations bill has lasted eight years. Changes were made at the proposals stage, the first bill stage, during House committee hearings and during the Senate committee hearings. I believe all who are familiar with the bill acknowledge that it is a very good bill. We have no illusions about developing a perfect bill that will please everyone and will resolve all problems. We think, therefore, parliament should consider the corporation law revision not as a secular process but, rather, as an annual process, to ensure that federal corporation law will not once again become as outdated as the present Canada Corporations Act.
Indeed, having already given the House committee an undertaking to crystallize at least one regulation as statute law within the next year, and knowing that further technical difficulties will arise as we acquire experience working with the bill, we will introduce a bill next year to deal with those issues. Through this process we compel the department to remain responsive to suggestions and also ensure that the law will be better adapted to changing economic and social conditions. As I said, the Senate committee in making its recommendations acted objectively, fairly and reasonably, arguing clearly and forcefully for each proposed amendment. I found it impossible not to be responsive to their suggestions, which I thought were consistent with the over-all development of this bill.
In conclusion, I repeat that this bill has been a long time in preparation. It is well structured, clearly drafted, comprehensive, imaginative and, above all, practical. I therefore urge all members of this House to support its passage.

I looked at the amendments while the hon. member for Edmonton West and the parliamentary secretary were speaking, and I found that six are so annoying that I must decline the parliamentary secretary's request to support the motion approving them. It strikes me that these are amendments we might expect from the other place. Frankly, I do not like them. I object to six amendments; two on page 136, two on page 137, one on page 139 and one on page 140. In all six cases the Senate wants to change the law so that action, if necessary, can be taken only against a corporation and not against its directors or officers. In every one of the six amendments to which I have referred, the original words "or its directors or officers" have been deleted.
Having listened to the soothing words of the parliamentary secretary, I was puzzled to discover that in two instances those words were actually written in the bill by the committee of this House which considered it. In other words, the inclusion of those words was not accidental; the bill which this House sent to the other place included the provision that in certain instances a conviction could be sought against a corporation or against its officers or directors. Considering the number of officers and directors sitting in the other place, I am not surprised by what has been done. They object to this provision in the law.
I have in mind the fact that in some countries in recent years it has been recognized that when companies break the law, the companies should suffer but so should some of the executives who are responsible for their decisions. Likewise, in this country we face what has been called the dredging scandal. I suggest that perhaps that scandal is not really within the confines of the government; it is a scandal within the confines of certain corporations. I suggest that when bad decisions are made by corporations, they are actually made by officers or directors of the corporations, and those officers or directors should be subject to the penalties of the law. Therefore, I do not like what the Senate did in deleting the references to directors or officers of companies in the six places to which I have referred.
Perhaps I shall find still other of the 27 amendments offensive. I must now say that the assurance I was given earlier, namely, that these amendments are administrative and need not cause us any concern, does not wash as far as I am concerned. So even if all I can do is shout "On division" when the question is put, that is what I shall do to register my opposition to the changes which the Senate made to the bill which the House of Commons sent to it.

subtopic: MEASURES TO PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH AND ENVIRONMENT FROM CONTAMINANTS

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 21, 1975, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp (for the Minister of the Environment) That Bill C-25, to protect human health and the environment from substances that contaminate the environment; be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Fairweather (p. 2251).

speakeroldname: Hon. Jeanne Sauve (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: MEASURES TO PROTECT HUMAN HEALTH AND ENVIRONMENT FROM CONTAMINANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank hon. members opposite for their very construction criticisms of this bill. I gladly accept these criticisms and I am certain that they will be very useful to me in administering the act when it is passed by the House.
I would have liked to reply point by point to some suggestions and the criticisms that have been made, but instead, I shall take advantage of the study of the bill by the committee on fisheries and forestry to do so. Today, I would simply like to say that when hon. members made suggestions about Bill C-25, they omitted to consider the other acts under which we may act to protect human health or the environment, which include the Hazardous Products Act, the Pest Control Products Act and the Clean Air Act, under which, I might mention, we must prove a real health hazard; all these acts enable us to take measures. However, we needed a new bill in which, as you will note, we ask only for residual powers to fill the gaps of certain federal and provincial acts.
As I have already explained, Bill C-25 concerns suspicious substances of which there might be traces in eco-systems. These are substances which are not biodegradable, and their accumulation may eventually have damaging effects on the environment or create health hazards. Mr. Speaker, we needed this new bill to deal with suspicious substances, which sometimes have minimal or indirect effects on health or the environment.
We had to obtain the authority to make additional studies on these substances which might be traced in the food chain, the life cycle or the atmosphere.
Some of those substances have already been identified. We mentioned freon, S02, cadmium and recently we discussed at length the indirect effects of asbestos fibres inhalation on the health of workers.
This measure is not of the same generation as those aimed at eradicating pollution, but it is a preventive measure. We shall identify suspicious substances and then analyze them. We want to check the presence of those substances in all kinds of manufactured products. This is why we are seeking this new authority.
The hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) feels that under this bill I should request information on every manufactured product. I am not sure whether the hon. member realizes the volume of paperwork that would be involved if I were to request information on each and every manufactured product. I believe their number totals 30,000 a year.

Environmental Contaminants Act
It is absolutely impossible to examine each one of these products within reasonable time. The processing of data would require a very large staff, because I would have to tell manufacturers within a reasonable time frame: You may now go ahead with the manufacturing of such or such a product, because close scrutiny showed that the manufactured products involved contain no suspicious substance that would affect the environment.
Therefore, I am seeking authority to request complete information on substances that we feel may constitute a danger. The hon. member for Rocky Mountain wonders how I will go about identifying such substances, and proposes, or rather he feels that I will rely on messages carried by birds.
Mr. Speaker, I love birds, and if by any chance they perched on my shoulder, as the hon. member suggested, I wish it were only to bring good news. I therefore will not trust birds to bring me information on suspicious substances. He knows very well I would not trust them. At any rate, I wish they kept on carrying good news about the environment.
I will know substances are suspicious from research work carried around the world. I named some of these substances: freon, cadmium, S02 and certain other products we feel may indirectly affect the environment or human health. As soon as we suspect one substance may be dangerous, we will endeavour to analyze it and find out which manufactured product uses it in order to know what quantity of this suspicious substance would thus be present in the environment, in eco-systems, in the food chain or in the atmosphere.
Therefore I must limit myself to such suspicious substances. I cannot examine all the chemicals that are manufactured in this country. Therefore, following such scientific research work, following the observations of scientists or medical doctors, we will decide whether the study of a certain substance or of a certain product should be advisable. Then, after we have gathered sufficient information, we will be able to enact regulations to limit their use and prohibit them if they are dangerous. We may also prohibit their export or regulate their use one way or the other.
The hon. member, in the same spirit, would also like me to give in the bill a list of these suspicious substances. I might be able to do it and I will consider his proposal. But here again, I should like to warn him about the danger of claiming without sufficient proof that such a substance is suspicious. After all, one should proceed with some caution in regulating the use of certain products because considerable damage could obviously be caused to industry that could not be justified afterwards. Therefore, I am only asking to be able to proceed with the caution normally shown by governments.
The hon. member says that all I am asking for is a complaints office. If I were, for instance, responsible for the police, I would only have a complaints office, and then, I would be unable to take action. I put this question to him: should I, as a result of complaints, put everyone in jail? That is precisely what I want to avoid. If I get complaints, I want to be able to look into them and then, request the authority to take action.

I should also like to deal with another aspect of the question. The hon. member claimed to be very concerned about the authority of the Environment Department. He objects to my consulting other departments, other government agencies, at the various stages of the studies I shall have to make of some of those substances. He sees weakness in the obligation I want to assume of consulting departments, agencies and provincial governments. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that is no indication of weakness. Might I remind the hon. member that the department and the Minister of the Environment hold their authority from the cabinet itself which, on December 20th, 1973, promulgated the policy whereby all government departments and agencies must seek the advice of the Department of the Environment on matters falling within its jurisdiction. Moreover, they must seek the advice of the Department of the Environment before undertaking any major project which might affect or have any bearing whatesoever on the environment.
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have answered briefly and, I am sure, completely the objections of the hon. members on the other side of the House to this bill being given second reading. I believe my explanations should suffice at this point in the study of the bill. Consequently, I suggest and request of the House that it pass the motion and refer Bill C-25 to the standing committee on fisheries and forestry for consideration. May I assure my hon. colleagues that at other stages of this bill I shall welcome any and all amendments or suggestions that conform with the spirit of the bill and can improve it.

speechtext:
that Bill C-56, to provide for the resumption and continuation of longshoring and related operations at ports on the west coast of Canada, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will be aware that the bill just introduced for second reading contains the government's legislative proposals respecting longshoring and related operations at ports on the west coast. I shall refer to these proposals in some detail a little later, but first it would be helpful and appropriate to recall some of
March 24, 1975

the pertinent background facts and events which have led to the introduction of these proposals.
The West Coast Ports Operations Act, 1975, has as its principal subject some 4,000 non-supervisory and supervisory longshoremen, represented by the International Longshoremen's and Warehousemen's Union, and the British Columbia Maritime Employers Association, representing some 61 companies. As hon. members realize, we are contending here with two distinctly separate yet related dispute situations. With respect to the non-supervisory longshoremen, who are represented by seven locals of the ILWU, a legal strike began on March 2 after unsuccessful attempts to negotiate a revision of their collective agreement which expired on December 31, 1974.
It should be pointed out that during negotiations both the union and the employer made firm recommendations that no conciliation board or conciliation commissioner should be appointed in these disputes. In fact, it was suggested by the parties that possibly conciliation board reports were partially to blame for past strikes in the port of Vancouver, as such reports were invariably rejected by one side or the other and a strike ensued. The parties felt confident that, if left to their own devices, settlement could be reached in direct negotiations without resort to strike or lockout. To give the parties full opportunity to work out a mutually arrived at settlement, the conciliation procedures were waived and the parties so notified on December 31, 1974.
The parties resumed direct negotiations early in the new year which reached an impasse, and on January 23 the union membership voted heavily in favour of strike action. Negotiations resumed following the taking of a strike vote on January 23, carried on for some time, and after a final week of very intensive negotiations an impasse was reached on March 1; on March 2 the union called a legal strike affecting dock operations at 11 ports: Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster, Prince Rupert, Nanaimo, Port Alberni, Chemainus, Harmac, Crofton, Cowichan Bay and Squamish.
Five days later, William Kelly, my department's assistant deputy minister for industrial relations, was appointed as mediator in the dispute and on March 16, following an intensive mediation session, succeeded in bringing the parties to a settlement-a settlement subject to ratification by the union membership. So at this stage there was reason for optimism, and particularly so when a union caucus of 55 delegates subsequently voted 67 per cent in favour of endorsing the terms of the settlement. However, as we now know, this was not the attitude of the union membership, of whom some 55 per cent voted to reject the mediated settlement. Thus, the strike continued and so, too, continued the disruption and damage not only to many sectors of the Canadian economy but also to those foreign countries suffering unfulfilled contracts, particularly grain contracts.
Talking of economic damage, as we know the Canadian Wheat Board has undertaken substantial commitments to many overseas customers, of whom Japan has already had to make alternative arrangements. Not only have our shipments fallen seriously behind-by some 60 million bushels
Longshoremen's Strike
during the current grain year-but our grain transportation facilities, the farmers and other sectors are now facing severe strains which cannot be permitted to continue.
In my opinion, the mediated settlement was a most reasonable settlement and I find it impossible to convince myself of the validity of its final rejection by the union membership. This rejected package provided for a wage increase of $1.95 an hour over two years, $1.15 in the first year and 80 cents in the second.
Members will agree that it is a most difficult decision for a Minister of Labour to conclude that collective bargaining has run its full course, that other measures must be taken to terminate a dispute having a serious effect on the economy of a nation, and in this instance having worldwide effects when starving people are asking for aid.

I would now refer to the second dispute situation involving 13 west coast stevedoring companies and the ship and dock foremen of local 514 of the ILWU. This case surrounds, in part, the application of local 514 for certification by the Canada Labour Relations Board and the parties' attempts to negotiate a first contract. Some eight months ago the union was certified by the board as bargaining agent for units of foremen of 12 or 13 companies. The exception at that time involved Pacific Coast Terminals Limited which was subsequently certified in January of this year.
However, these certifications shortly became the subject of proceedings instituted in the Federal Court by the employers against the decisions of the Canada Labour Relations Board. Nonetheless, the parties held separate and joint meetings in direct negotiations which were unsuccessful to the extent that a conciliation officer was appointed to deal with the 13 collective bargaining disputes. Again-and I am still talking about the foremen-a settlement was not to be forthcoming and the union had the right to strike as of January 8. No further conciliation efforts were advanced. Further inability to reach an agree-
4424

Longshoremen's Strike
ment culminated March 22 in the foremen setting up picket lines at all 13 company locations involved.
I have already briefly referred to the damaging situation which now exists as a result of the first mentioned strike. That this situation cannot be allowed to continue is selfevident. Therefore, the West Coast Ports Operations Act, 1975, orders the immediate resumption of both non-supervisory and supervisory longshoring and related operations.
With respect to the strike of non-supervisory employees, their strike will cease immediately on the coming into force of this legislation and they will return to work under the terms of their collective agreement which expired December 31, 1974. This extended collective agreement will expire on December 31, 1976, or whenever a new agreement or an amended agreement comes into force before that date. No strike or lockout is to be permitted during the entire term of this extended agreement. An arbitrator is to be appointed to whom will be referred all matters relating to the amendment and revision of the collective agreement that are in dispute. The arbitrator's decisions, together with other amendments previously agreed to by the parties, will constitute a new collective agreement that will be in effect from January 1, 1975.
With respect to the dispute involving the supervisory employees of local 514, their right to strike will cease immediately on the coming into force of this legislation and they will also return to work on the same terms and conditions that applied before the work stoppage. No company may alter any term or condition without union agreement. No strike or lockout is to be permitted prior to the establishment of a collective agreement. An arbitrator is to be appointed to whom will be referred all matters that are in dispute between the companies and the union.
That, Mr. Speaker, is in essence my remarks and I would ask for the approval of this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in beginning may I say as clearly as I can that it is a matter of deep regret that once again parliament is called upon to legislate back to work workers who are legally on strike. I am sure all hon. members would wish it were otherwise, but the fact remains that in the absence of effective procedures to resolve disputes between management and labour that affect the national interest, legislation of this nature is not only necessary, it is inevitable. It is inevitable because there comes a point when the rights of the parties to a dispute-I refer especially to the right of lockout and the right to strike-can no longer be permitted to trespass on that greater right shared by all of the public, that irreparable damage to the national interest cannot be permitted to continue.
I recognize that it is not always easy to resolve the ever present conflict between the two positions. This is a free country and Canadians have recognized that a part of that freedom is the right to strike in furtherance of the demands of working people in this country. But no right is absolute in a civil society. I know this is recognized by the majority of labour leaders. I believe it is recognized by the vast majority of the millions of Canadians who make up the work force of this nation.
What has not been recognized by this government is that it has an obligation to establish a coherent procedure which will result in a fair wage and fair conditions of work without recourse to crippling strikes that deny essential services and drive destructively at the very substance of the national interest. As all members know, a public interest disputes commission has long been advocated by this party. The government response is that it will not work; but to date the government has offered nothing in its place. If the past few years have shown anything, it has been that in the absence of some agreement between management, labour and government whereby all three accept the responsibility to avoid the intolerable effects of certain strikes on the national interest, parliament will be recalled again and again to resolve the difficulty on an ad hoc basis.
This self-evident truth is, in fact, shared by all political parties. The Liberal government has either invoked existing legislation or introduced special legislation four times since August, 1972, to restore grain movements, shipping and transportation. During the debate in 1973 to restore rail movement, the then leader of the New Democratic Party said:
We, of course, agree that parliament has a duty to the people of Canada and to the public interest, and that there comes a point in a strike such as a national railway strike at which members of parliament must take the responsibility of making certain that rail operations are resumed so that the harm, the difficulties, the hardship caused by the strike are ended.
Recently, in British Columbia, the NDP premier of that province tossed all his former rhetoric to the winds and swiftly introduced legislation ending a strike of municipal firemen. He knew, and everyone knew, that an essential service cannot be withdrawn. It is easy to say it is difficult to determine what is an essential service or what is destructive of the national interest, but this argument is nonsense and is refuted by the practice of all governments, of whatever political stripe, acting by legislation in such cases. The tragedy is that so often so much damage is done when it could be averted before the event. But this will not happen until all of us in Canada face the facts of life and adjust our bargaining procedures accordingly. Real freedom is only enjoyed within civil society. Chaos is not freedom; it is the breakdown of a civil society and it creates a climate where, in desperation, people will cry for order even at the expense of their liberties.
Clearly, in the case before us, the national interest is gravely affected. It is in the national interest that Canada deliver its grain shipments, and on time. It is also in the national interest that the grain producers of Canada obtain the best price for that grain. As hon. members know, the inability to meet our delivery commitments has resulted in the grain producers being caught in a falling price situation, and this loss is borne not by the nation at large but by one segment of the nation.
The demurrage charges, mounting in the millions, are paid for by the grain producers. The hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) chided us for speaking of grain last Wednesday last. The fact is that last Wednesday we had every expectation that the longshoremen's strike would be settled satisfactorily, and there was no need to talk about the great damage to other sectors of the economy if the ports were closed. That is now the unhappy

March 24, 1975

result; but it was proper that hon. members made cleai how unfair it is to allow one group in Canada to suffer the largest portion of economic loss.
I remind all hon. members that no grain has moved since February 17. For several weeks the ports have been closed to all shipping. Ninety-three ships are now waiting for cargoes on the west coast. Since August 1, 1974, over 40 per cent of all ordinary grain loading days have been lost because of work stoppages. Increasingly, other workers- not involved in the dispute are being laid off as a direct result of the strikes. It is not just that there is now a national emergency; the national interest has been disastrously affected for many weeks, and during this long time the government has stood by, mouthing platitudes about the right to strike while the damage to the national interest mounted day by day.
Apart completely from the government's long inability to devise better procedures for settling industrial disputes, the effect of inflation is directly affecting the entire climate of negotiations. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) knows, because he has said it often enough, inflation threatens the very fabric of our society. It is not difficult to understand why workers, especially those at the lower end of the pay scale, are demanding what seem to be absolutely incredible percentage increases. But the reason is plain: they have no confidence in the future.
It is not hard to understand why usually quiescent unions are now militant, and it ought not to be wondered at that a concomitant of lack of confidence is a rank and file refusal to abide by the recommendations of their own negotiating teams. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said in September:
Whether we succeed in realizing our great potential depends mainly on ourselves. One way or another a balance is going to be struck in the allocation of shares of the national income between the various sectors of the economy. We can come together and seek to strike a fair and reasonable balance between such elements as wages, prices and profits through a process of consensus which will make possible continued strong growth of national income to the benefit of us all. Alternatively, we can allow the balance to be determined by the process of prolonged and bitter industrial strife, which could leave everyone considerably worse off by substantially reducing the size of the pie that is available to be shared between us.
It ought to be obvious that we are now, in fact, experiencing just what the Minister of Finance predicted. But he made that speech in September. The months have passed. The search for the elusive consensus continues; but incredibly those who are being consulted have no idea whatsoever what the government believes is a "fair and reasonable balance". We have no idea what the government's objectives are. But one thing is so terribly clear: seven months after the Minister of Finance's speech the government is still refusing to show any leadership. Perhaps this is borne from a sense of impotence or an inability to take the tough decisions that are needed. I suggest it is also due to a sense of unwarranted pessimism on the part of the government which reveals a certain lack of faith in Canadians to meet a challenge.
Last year the Prime Minister responded to the crisis of inflation with the warning: You cannot ask for common restraint because people will not co-operate. Certainly some people will cheat on their neighbours, but we have
Longshoremen's Strike
not been, and are not now, a nation of cheaters; and we are not a nation of cowards unable to brace ourselves to accept our responsibilities.
Recently, responding to the deepening crisis in the economy, the Prime Minister complained that it is difficult to do anything because nobody trusts the government any more. Certainly the government has to have the trust of the public, to lead effectively. But its own determined action must be the basis of the trust. This government recently received a majority mandate. The Prime Minister has been treated very generously by the people of Canada and instead of complaining about some undefined meanness in our national spirit he should start employing the good will his government still enjoys before it is wasted on the barren ground of timidity.
Mr. Speaker, there is no question that we are faced with a national emergency. What is required is a national response. Every Canadian is involved in that response. The measure of the civility of our society is very much at stake now and will be in the coming months. Leadership is called for, not just from the government but from the leaders of all parts of our society.
My party supports this bill today because it is necessary to do so. But we also say to the Prime Minister, show us what you wish to accomplish; give us some idea of how you wish us to respond; make it clear to all Canadians that the best is being demanded of us, not the worst. I say to the right hon. gentleman, through you, Mr. Speaker, that we will not be found wanting.

Mr. Speaker, it is no surprise to anyone in our country to learn that the NDP, whether at the federal level or at the provincial level, has a profound disposition to oppose legislation that forces working men and women back to work under any circumstances. We believe that one of the essential aspects of a free society is the right of men and women to withdraw their services if they feel that the circumstances under which they are working are unsatisfactory to them. It is the basic right of any free society, and it must only be with the greatest degree of reluctance that any person or party committed to this idea would support legislation involving the abridgement of this basic right, because that is exactly what is involved and we in parliament have to face the situation if that course of action is taken.
The only possible circumstance under which, in our view, there would be justification for taking away this fundamental right would be something that would come under the rubric of the national interest. The national interest, like nationalism and a number of other concepts, is used frequently to disguise quite perfidious kinds of actions, so that when you say you are acting in the national interest it seems to me there is a basic obligation to spell out in some detail at least what you have in mind.
I am now saying, on behalf of our party, that we will support this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, a special piece of legislation was adopted by this Parliament in October 1974 to deal with a labour dispute, namely to force striking grain handlers in western ports back to work and extend the term of their collective agreement to November 1975.
At that time, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) made practically the same statement as today. He introduced a measure to deal with a somewhat unusual situation and force workers back to work, claiming that he was acting in the best interests of Canada.
I remember taking part in the debate and supporting the legislation in the interest of all Canadians, while deploring the fact that Parliament had to intervene again in a labour dispute.
Last week, we had a special debate on a labour dispute on the west coast. During this debate, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) stated most emphatically that Parliament had no intention whatever of depriving workers of the right to strike which Parliament itself had granted to them. Speaking about workers he said, for instance, as one can read on page 4276 of Hansard:
Me. Chretien: Parliament gave them that right, and I believe in collective bargaining. What has happened in respect of this strike is another example of the fact that if you are patient enough you can resolve problems.

In addition to that, even if I had settled that strike last week, or at the beginning of this week, it would have done absolutely nothing to change the situation in respect of wheat movement out of the port of Vancouver, because the longshoremen were on strike and I have no responsibility for them.

Therefore "next week" is now and we still have this strike which still goes on, as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) predicted.
Now it is not out of sheer wantonness, I know, that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) introduces a measure to force the workers, who go on strike legally and are using a right which was granted to them, to go back to work, even if negotiations go on, if they continue to try to find an agreement so that the Vancouver port and western ports may be kept busy, and that our international trade may not suffer too many losses.
Now there is once more evidence of the existence of conflicts throughout Canada. We feel as though we were on a volcano. As soon as a strike is settled in one area, others flare up and the fight goes on, which shows again the uneaseness that exists between the rights recognized by government authorities as to labour capital and money capital. I have the clear impression that the government is braver when it has to pass legislation concerning labour capital than when it deals with financial interests.
For once I would like to go at the bottom of things instead of laying all the blames on workers. As for the indexation formula, we hear little else these days. Driving from my home to Ottawa earlier today, I heard a 90-minute radio program during which reference was made to indexation. I do not at all believe in that formula as an effective solution to our problems. We do not yet have any proof. When salary increases are granted to a group of workers, because prices are continuing to rise, the industries or companies which pay higher salaries boost their prices. It is not the sole cause of price increases, there are also other causes which will have to be analyzed. Salaries are not the only cause of the cost of living increase, of inflation, but it is one of them.
Under the circumstances, workers who are not guaranteed better wages or are not assured that their income tax will be reduced, exert some pressures and use the strike to try and have their rights acknowledged. And you have to do it again after some time. It is always the same story, you have to do it again. Therefore indexing is not an appropriate system.
Now, I ask the Minister of Labour to have his officials make a close examination of the relations between labour capital and money capital in this industry, and to ensure that there be a fair share, so that companies do not grow

Mr. Speaker, recognizing that this measure has to be dealt with quickly I was not going to take part in the debate, but the interjection by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) when the House leader of this party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), was speaking makes me feel that the government probably has not realized the full implication of the suggestion the hon. member was putting forth.
Let me try very simply to put the situation as we see it. In a democratic society we always walk the tight-rope between two very basic democratic principles. The first is that those who earn their living by selling their labour have a right to bargain collectively regarding the price that they will get for the work they do. Ever since Abraham Lincoln freed the slaves on this continent, no person has been compelled to work against his or her will. People have the right to band themselves together in associations for the purpose of negotiating regarding the wages they will receive, the hours they will work and the conditions under which they will labour. This has been recognized by all parties in this House and by the majority of Canadian people as a basic right of a free people.
Against that we always have to balance the harm which it does to society as a whole if a labour dispute ends in a strike which carries on for a considerable period of time. There seems to have been a mistaken idea in some quarters that workers enjoy going on strike. I walked the picket lines when I was a young printer. Mr. Speaker, it is no fun being on strike. Not only does the employer lose business, not only is society inconvenienced, but the worker is going without wages; he suffers because of the strike. Men and women do not easily go on strike. They do not go on strike because it is a lot of fun; they go on strike because they are convinced that the wages they are receiving and the terms and conditions under which they work are not fair and just.

It is true, as the House leader of this party has said, that there comes a time when a long industrial dispute harms the community as a whole to the point where it must be brought to an end. We agree that this is a situation where a strike has to be ended. We support the idea, under these circumstances, of having legislation passed by this parliament which will bring this strike to an end. But the point which I think the government has not become sufficiently seized of is that when you take from a group of workers in this country the basic right to withhold their services, then you must put in its place the basis for fair and just settlement.
Compulsory arbitration is the court of last resort. Compulsory arbitration means that a group of workers will allow another individual whom they did not select, but who is appointed by the government, to decide what price they will get for their labour for the next two years. That is tremendous authority to place in the hands of an individual. If you take from these workers their right to withhold their labour; if you say, as this legislation does, they must go back to work, surely you must give them some guarantees: you must guarantee that you are not using the excuse of the national interest to deprive them of a fair and just settlement.
In the process of this strike, which has lasted several weeks, the workers made demands and the employers made offers. Finally a partial settlement was reached. The employers made an offer which the bargaining committee for the union accepted but which the union membership repudiated. This legislation says to the workers, "You must go back to work." But on what terms are they to go back? The terms are those of a bargaining agreement 2'A years old which expired on December 31 last. The workers could not get an agreement from their employers which, in the opinion of the workers, offered satisfactory wages and conditions.
I think the least parliament can do is say to the workers, "We are ordering you back to work, but we guarantee that the minimum you will receive is what the employer was willing to pay." According to figures I saw in newspapers-I have no inside information-the employers are willing to pay an additional $1.85 an hour more over a two-year period. If they are willing to pay that, what right have we to order men back to work on the basis of an agreement signed 2Vi years ago? An arbitrator could decide that the employees will receive less wages than the employers offered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the intent of the motion is clear. The proposal before us calls upon the government to consider the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act in order to provide benefits to all spouses of old age security pensioners who have not reached the age of 65. The implications of this proposition are evident. Under the terms of the motion, such non-pensioner spouses would become eligible for the basic pension which currently is $123.42 per month. In addition, eligible married couples would become entitled to the guaranteed income supplement if their joint income required support. The present maximum supplement level for a married couple comes to $76.88 each a month.
The ultimate purpose of the motion can be interpreted as the provision of additional income support to a substantial number of Canadians. I might point out that this very end is one which the federal government has actively pursued: the Government of Canada has been firmly com-
March 24, 1975

mitted to the principle of ensuring that all Canadians can live in dignity. Various social security plans have been enacted to support the incomes of those least able to provide for themselves. In some cases, benefits have been granted to everyone in a designated group, on a universal basis. The old age security pension is the best example of this sort of program. In other instances, allowances have been given only to those in need. The Canada Assistance Plan constitutes the major scheme of this type in Canada today.
Despite varied modalities of operation, the objective of these programs has been the alleviation of economic distress across the country. Unfortunately, this situation has tended to be pronounced among the elderly as a group in Canadian society. Therefore, the welfare of senior citizens has been of special concern to the government.
Over the years, the federal government has endeavoured constantly to come to terms with the problems confronting our senior citizens. I need only refer hon. members to the establishment of the old age pension plan in 1927, with the co-operation of the provinces, and the creation of the old age security pension program in 1952. These measures are indicative of the resolute action taken by the Government of Canada to resolve difficulties faced by the elderly at different points in our history.
Today, the old age security pension, the universal entitlement, is the base upon which senior citizens rely for their financial support. This program is the focal point of government effort to assist Canadians in their old age. Aware of the role of this scheme in the lives of our senior citizens, the government has striven to adapt the plan to meet the changing requirements of the elderly.
Undoubtedly, the most important changes in the Old Age Security Act have dealt with eligibility and benefit levels. Originally, the requirement was 20 years of residence in Canada immediately preceding the approval of an application for the pension. It was recognized, however, that there would be people who might have lived in this country for a good many years earlier in their lives and who would return to Canada to spend their remaining years after being away for some time. It was felt that the contributions made to this country by such persons should not be overlooked, and that they should not be deprived of pension rights.
A second method of qualifying was therefore devised, permitting persons who had been present in Canada prior to those 20 years for at least twice the length of their period of absence during the basic 20 years to qualify for the pension, provided they had resided in Canada for one full year immediately preceding the day on which their application was approved. In 1957, the basic period of residence was reduced from 20 to 10 years. It followed that the period of make-up time required was correspondingly reduced. In 1965, a third method of qualifying, on the basis of 40 years of residence after the age of 18, was added.
Residence requirements now enable pensions to be paid to applicants who fulfil one of the following criteria: first, having resided in Canada, after attaining the age of 18, for periods which total at least 40 years; second, having resided in Canada for the ten years immediately preceding the approval of an application; third, having been present in Canada, after reaching age 18 and prior to the ten years
Longshoremen's Strike
mentioned above, for periods which equal, when totalled, at least three times the length of absence during the ten-year period and having resided in Canada for at least one year immediately preceding the approval of an application.
In addition, provision was made to permit the payment of benefits outside of Canada to pensioners who have resided in Canada for a total of 20 years after the age of 18.
I should add that pensioners who are absent from Canada for a period of up to six months and do not meet this requirement may still receive their old age security. This provision was introduced to permit pensioners without long histories of residence here to take vacations and to avoid the severe Canadian winters.
Another important change was the reduction of the age of eligibility from 70 to 65. The 1965 amendment to the Old Age Security Act provided for the progressive lowering of the age of entitlement one year at a time. In January, 1970, the age requirement reached 65. Nevertheless, perhaps the most noteworthy innovation regarding the Old Age Security Act in the 1960s was the establishment of the guaranteed income supplement to the old age security pension in 1967. This measure can be attributed to the awareness by the government of the unfavourable financial state in which many of our senior citizens have found themselves in recent years. Because of the harsh realities of the depression and the wars, a substantial proportion of Canadians lacked the opportunity to make adequate provision for their old age. In addition, a large number of pensioners were employed in occupations or businesses not covered by private pension plans or superannuation schemes.
The guaranteed income supplement has been paid to pensioners with no income, or only a limited amount of income, for over eight years. This income support has been based solely on an income test; all that is required is a declaration of income somewhat similar to that required for a tax return. I should emphasize that an incentive plan was built into this scheme to avoid causing prejudice to individuals who have made some financial provision for their old age. Supplements have been paid to pensioners to bring their income to a guaranteed minimum. This level currently comes to $209.99 per month for single pensioners, and $200.30 a month each for a married couple. Total supplements have been reduced by only $1 for each $2 of additional income received. With this method of calculating guaranteed income supplement benefits, Canadians have been encouraged to plan financially for their retirement years.
The government has continued to improve income security programs for the elderly. I need only refer to measures enacted within the past few years. As members of this House no doubt remember, the basic old age security pension was increased from $82.88 to $100 effective April, 1973. Moreover, parliament approved legislation in September, 1973, to make benefits under the Old Age Security Act more responsive to the cost of living by adjusting payments quarterly rather than annually. As a result, pensions are now protected against the effects of inflation. Five increases have brought the basic monthly old age security pension from $100 in October, 1973, to $123.42

effective April, 1975. I should stress that guaranteed income supplement benefits have progressed in a similar proportion.
As far as the future is concerned, I draw the attention of the House to the Speech from the Throne that opened this session of parliament. The government intends to introduce legislation to provide for the payment of allowances, on an income tested basis, to spouses aged 60 to 65 of recipients of the old age security pension. This proposal represents an extension of the government's effort to meet the ever evolving needs of senior citizens. With the cooperation of the House, this proposal will become effective later this year.
In this context, therefore, the motion being deliberated should be examined critically. The most obvious shortcoming of this proposal is the fact that the government has already announced its intention to introduce a spouse's allowance. The intended amendment to the Old Age Security Act is ample proof of the due consideration given by the government to this question.
In proposing this amendment to the Old Age Security Act, the government is aware that not all spouses of old age security pensioners who are under the age of 65 will be covered. However, while appreciating the desire of the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) to make the old age security pension more comprehensive, I feel obligated to make the following observations. When considering any extension of social security benefits, the government must take into account its financial resources in relation to its priorities. In addition to the difficulties of pensioners and their spouses, the problems of the disabled, the one-parent families, the working poor and other disadvantaged groups also have to be considered. This is the crux of the matter: because the government must look after the interests of all Canadians, it is required to take a global view in dealing with questions relating to social security. While the old age security program is one of the important ingredients in Canada's social security framework, it must be considered in perspective with other essential elements.
Moreover, the rights of the provinces in the area of social security must also be taken into account. I should remind hon. members that a joint federal-provincial review of the entire social security structure is under way at the present time. The federal government has made its position on this crucial issue clear in its "Working paper on social security in Canada", released in April, 1973. As some hon. members may recall, this orange paper represented a framework of 5 strategies and 14 propositions set out within these categories as the federal government's contribution to the present appraisal of social security. The outcome of this federal-provincial review will influence the future of all social security measures. However, as the needs of the elderly change in response to shifting economic and social forces, the federal government will continue to develop measures to meet the evolving requirements of our senior citizens.
Nevertheless, for the short term at least the Government of Canada has reserved the right to introduce interim adjustments to social security programs to come to terms with the more pressing needs of Canadians. It is in this context that the federal government intends to amend the Old Age Security Act to provide allowances to spouses

aged 60 to 65 of old age security pensioners. With concrete action such as this, it is indeed evident that this government is ever mindful of the requirements of the aged.

I must say that when the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) stood up I had hoped he would make a contribution to this debate. I do not deny that the government has taken action. It has taken action in certain fields concerning social services. It should take action. This is the reason why the hon. member for Abitibi had to come forward with this motion. There is another matter that we must always bear in mind, and that is the automatic reduction to 50 per cent of the pension benefits. As to the expenditures involved, I think the hon. member who proposed this resolution-and I do not wish to speak for him-should at least be ready to consider the notion that some of the wasteful programs in which the government indulges might be cut back for the benefit of those who have built our society and given it to us in its present form. It is those who are no longer able to make their contribution economically to our society for whom we should have the greater concern. It is those who are beyond the strength and the age to make that contribution whom we must consider in this context.

This matter has been considered by the federal government, and promises in this area have been made in the Speech from the throne.
I should like to add one further comment to what the previous speaker has just said. He mentioned our older people, our senior citizens, our grandmothers and our grandfathers. I think it is only fair to say of them that throughout this country we find in them some of the finest teachers that are available to the young people of Canada today. I hope other schemes can be considered that will put a vast amount of knowledge that has been stored by our senior citizens to a more creative use. I am referring to knowledge about finance, about business, about engineering, and many other aspects of knowledge that we of the younger generation, as well as our children, can use to greatest advantage in the future.
To ensure a balanced debate on the motion under consideration I believe it is necessary to discuss the various measures already developed by the federal government which benefit the elderly. While these programs and policies are by themselves different, they form part of the comprehensive strategy evolved by the government which meets the changing needs of senior citizens.
Perhaps the most important programs relate to ensuring the physical and mental well-being of the aged. Because of the excellent degree of co-operation between the federal government and the provinces in the area of health care, Canada's system of health insurance provides a high level of medical care to senior citizens. Since the establishment of medicare in 1968 with the joint intervention of the federal and provincial levels of government, the elderly in Canada have enjoyed the advantages of comprehensive coverage at little or no cost to them. No longer do senior citizens have to wait to seek care because they cannot afford it. No longer should a serious illness or accident pose a financial catastrophe for either an individual or a family as a whole.
As a consequence of medicare the elderly in Canada have peace of mind which comes from knowing that they enjoy virtually unlimited access to competent medical assistance in times of illness or infirmity. Because senior citizens have a greater tendency than other age groups of Canadians to become afflicted with long-term ailments, they have benefited enormously under medicare.
There are no limits to the number of days of necessary hospital care. There are no ceilings on the frequency of visits to physicians. In addition, no individual Canadian is subject to a personal dollar quota of entitlement to health
care.
Another feature of particular concern to the elderly is the involvement of the federal government in the provision of residential care for senior citizens who are ill or infirm. It is a very important type of program being set up by the government in this respect. Under the terms of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act of 1957, the government of Canada has entered into cost-sharing arrangements with the provinces to establish specialized nursing homes, infirmaries, or similar institutions geared to the requirements of the elderly. This scheme has proved
March 24, 1975

of inestimable value to the chronically ill and infirm across Canada.
In the area of housing great strides have been made to provide decent accommodation for the aged. Under the National Housing Act the federal government has actively promoted the construction of new dwellings and the repair and modernization of existing housing. This is of great importance to many areas of our country, including some areas in my riding, and areas in the far north where housing can now be brought closer to some form of a decent living standard.
Assistance for the construction of subsidized public housing has constituted an essential element of this program as well. On a shared-cost basis with the provinces and municipalities the federal government has financed the construction of public housing units and hostel accommodation which has given proper shelter to disadvantaged senior citizens.
In addition, with the co-operation of provincial and municipal governments as well as private entrepreneurs, the Government of Canada has made accommodation available to Canadians on a rent-to-income basis. Senior citizens who cannot afford open market rentals and who are ineligible for public housing have benefited greatly from this scheme as well.
Moreover, the National Housing Act has provided direct subsidies to low-income homeowners for the rehabilitation of private sub-standard dwellings in areas selected for neighbourhood improvement, which takes in the large cities. Eligible senior citizens have found this provision of value to them as well.
The Canada Assistance Plan represents another essential element in Canada's social security framework of benefit to the aged. This scheme complements aspects of social security measures which are currently not covered by specific federal legislation.
The Canada Assistance Plan is the vehicle by which the federal government shares with the provinces the cost of specified assistance to economically disadvantaged Canadians on a 50-50 basis. The granting of aid is determined by a needs or budget deficit test which takes into consideration a person's requirements in relation to his or her available resources. Through the establishment of national norms the Canada Assistance Plan has enabled recipients to maintain a decent standard of living with the help of programs administered directly by the provinces. As a result of its single administrative infrastructure the Canada Assistance Plan has been able to respond with flexibility to the changing requirements of Canadians.
An important facet of the Canada Assistance Plan relates to supplementary medical benefits. The provinces may provide medical aid excluded under the terms of medicare to eligible Canadians in order to ensure their physical and mental well-being. As we grow older our physical well-being is of prime importance, but our mental well-being is of the utmost importance. Prescription drugs, eyeglasses, hearing aids, and even transportation to and from treatment centres are many of the items relating to medical care covered on a shared-cost basis between the Government of Canada and the provinces.
