Moreover, certain forms of residential care which are excluded under the terms of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act are also subsidized by the Canada Assistance Plan. This is for persons who are deemed by the provincial governments to be in need. The establishments, maintenance and operation of nursing homes and residences for the aged, sponsored by the federal government on a 50 per cent basis, has benefited senior citizens enormously. As a result the elderly have been provided with the means with which to live in dignity.
It should be added that the Canada Assistance Plan permits the provinces to provide income support to senior citizens in addition to benefits available under the current income security programs. With such supplementation the elderly can meet minimum personal budgetary requirements essential to a decent level of living. Perhaps I should call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned at five o'clock I was pointing out that the legislation before us asked parliament to give to the government very extraordinary powers-powers to send men back to work and place in the hands of a government appointed arbitrator the whole question of what their income will be for themselves, their wives and their families, for the next two years. Those are very extensive powers. They are powers which we do not exercise with respect to any other group in our society.
We do not tell manufacturers that they have to sell their commodity at a certain price and that they cannot withhold it from the market if they do not get the price they want. We do not tell farmers or any other group in our society that they cannot withhold their product but must sell it at a price set by someone else.

March 24, 1975
Longshoremen's Strike
In the case of workers in an emergency situation such as the one we have here, parliament takes upon itself the power to send workers back to the job and asks them to leave to someone appointed by the government the right to determine the wages and conditions under which they will work. I say that that is a very extraordinary power. And yet in this particular circumstance, and there have been other similar circumstances, the effect of a strike is so harmful to the nation as a whole, so detrimental to the national interest that parliament has been justified in taking such a step. In the particular instance before us we in the New Democratic Party feel that parliament is justified in bringing this strike to an end in order that the people who have been adversely affected by it may get some amelioration of their condition.
The plea I have been making is that in wielding this extraordinary power we ought to do it with all the justice and all the fairness of which we are capable. During the supper hour I listened to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) on a television clip saying he was most reluctant to introduce legislation like this. I suppose he is reluctant; I am sure we are all reluctant about having to resort to legislation which imposes compulsory arbitration.
All I am pleading for with the minister is that he accompany his reluctance with a measure which will at least give to the workers who are being sent back to their jobs a feeling that we recognize that they have a measure of justice on their side and that, as a result of this legislation, they will not get less income during the next two years than they would have received if they had stayed out on strike and forced a settlement.
I do not suppose any arbitrator appointed by the government would be so insensitive to the situation that he would bring down a settlement which would give to the workers less than was offered last week by the employers. But we have no guarantee of that, Mr. Speaker. The government has no guarantee of it. Once the government appoints an arbitrator under this legislation the matter is entirely out of its hands. That arbitrator will be able to set wages and conditions of labour that, under this bill, automatically become the collective bargaining agreement for the two years 1975 and 1976.
I cannot imagine any arbitrator being so stupid as to bring down legislation which would give these workers less than they have already been offered and less than they have rejected. But the Minister of Labour has no guarantee of that, I have no guarantee of that, and no other member of the House has any guarantee of it. What we are urging is that when we get into committee of the whole the government should give very serious consideration to stipulating some minimum figure which the workers will get irrespective of the decisions of the government arbitrator.
I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that when employers and employees begin to bargain on any collective agreement they usually start out with the employees asking for a fairly high increase and the employers offering a very low increase. During the process of negotiation they come closer and closer together. In hundreds upon hundreds of cases throughout this country every year they keep coming closer together, until they get a settlement without any strike.

We make a great deal of fuss about strikes. Certainly they are unsettling and none of us like to see them, but we forget that there are hundreds upon hundreds of agreements settled by peaceful negotiation between employer and employee. However, there are times when they get fairly close together but are not able to close the gap. When they cannot close the gap, then we have a strike.
When we force compulsory arbitration it seems to me that what ought to be submitted for arbitration is the gap between what the workers have asked for in their final submission and what the employer has offered in his final submission. It is much easier for an arbitrator to arbitrate the gap between the two competing parties than it is to do what this legislation does, send them back to square one and let them start all over again.
If the government were to accept our proposal and put in this legislation a provision that the arbitrator would start with what the companies offer as a floor, the arbitrator might well decide that the companies have offered all that is fair and reasonable. He may decide the union's bargaining committee were wise in accepting that offer and, therefore, that there is no additional money coming as a result of arbitration. Surely, if he is to decide they are entitled to more, he will decide after an exhaustive examination of the situation. Only then will he decide that workers are entitled to more than was offered. If our proposal is accepted, the workers being forced back to work will know they will not be deprived of gains they made in negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Liberal party has moved to the right far enough, and should not be invited to move any farther to the right.
If hon. members who interrupted me by saying workers don't want to work want to demonstrate the truth of their statement, let them take part in this debate. I doubt if they can demonstrate the correctness of their statement.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) a while ago asked if it is possible to devise a technique for eliminating strikes. I am sure everyone would be glad if a technique for eliminating strikes could be devised, particularly strikes in key industries. We, in my party, have never believed that imposing compulsory arbitration on workers is a satisfactory way of preventing strikes. In the final analysis, you can pass laws but you cannot make men and women work unless they feel they are working under fair conditions for fair and reasonable wages.
Many countries have tried to find the solution to industrial disputes, and Sweden has probably come closer to success than any other country. Sweden has not experienced a major strike since the 1930's. I do not suggest we can transplant the Swedish System to Canada; conditions are different. But we can learn important lessons from the Swedes. They have restructured their society, set up labour courts which are acceptable both to employer and employee and, most important, introduced a system of income distribution under which workers know they are getting a fair share of increased productivity and increased national wealth. If this government, this country, makes sure that workers and farmers get a fair share of our wealth production, we will see fewer industrial strikes.
But when workers read in the newspapers about the astronomical increases in profits which have taken place in this country in the last two or three years and then see their real incomes shrinking-the Canadian Labour Congress delegation to the government this morning pointed
Longshoremen's Strike
out that the incomes of many workers in real dollars have actually shrunk in the last three years-it is not surprising they go on strike. We will get rid of strikes only when we improve our system of social justice and bring about more equity in this country.

We agree, as our vote just indicated, with the principle involved, that of bringing the strike to an end. That is not in dispute. What makes us unhappy about the bill is that there is no guarantee that the minimum wage settlement agreed to by the negotiating parties will result from the award of the arbitrator. The minister's argument in reply to our general suggestion was that if parliament legislated a base, this would undermine the collective bargaining process. I say that the minister's argument would have force if parliament were legislating a total package.
If the whole range of issues in dispute and negotiated by the two parties were used as a base, then of course it follows that none of the workers in any collective bargaining unit would be willing to accept any agreement negotiated by their own negotiators, because they would rely on the final stamp of parliament which would establish a base rate-this is the logic used by the minister-and

If we should impair that system by amendments of this kind to the point where even further resort to parliament might be had in the future, then I cannot think of anything that the enemies of free collective bargaining would resort to more quickly in terms of trying to find a substitute method of resolving disputes. I still feel this is the best way, and I am sure hon. members opposite agree with that.
Having said that, let me indicate that although we cannot agree with this particular amendment of the NDP regarding $1.15 for the first year, this is not to say that we are not concerned that the men and women employees should be treated fairly in the circumstances. In all sincerity, let me tell the leader of the NDP that the forthcoming amendment that he has indicated he will move, setting a time limit for the arbitrator to render a decision, is still the most satisfactory way of accomplishing this.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this may be the first of a number of bills of a similar nature that will have to be moved, and I think we should look closely at some of the problems which were outlined earlier in the day. The question has been asked, with some justification, whether this type of legislation sending people back to work is required because of the commodity involved, the national interest, or the predominance of a particular area? I think the problem is much larger, Mr. Speaker, and I believe if this legislation is successful tonight members will ask the question, why? I do not think that most of the unions or most of the companies in this country want to negotiate by legislation. That, of course, would be an easy way to settle labour disputes.
A number of things are wrong with the legislation we now have, and with the system as well. People in the street are probably saying what a great thing it is that the Post Office strike is over but, Mr. Speaker, the Post Office strike has not started yet, although it probably will in the near future. But the public is so poorly informed that people do not know whether a strike is taking place in one area or another.
I have been concerned, as everyone else has, with Canada's reputation in regard to moving wheat. Problems in this area over the years have been solved by the establishment of a controller. When things have been really bad a controller has been able to settle problems in a matter of a few months because he has had jurisdiction over the whole transportation system as it affects wheat from the country elevator to loading the ship. That has worked in the past.
I think we should look at the whole structure of moving commodities in this country. It is likely that the present grouping is not the correct one. In the last two or three weeks the longshoremen have been on strike, and the government has said, "Let's not settle the public service strike". As long as the longshoremen were negotiating there was no point in settling the strike of the weighers and graders of grain because the grain was not going to move anyway. But there is a relationship between these two fields, Mr. Speaker. I think we should take all steps to prevent having to solve these problems by legislation.
Certainly parliament can force parties to accept the terms of an agreement. But should parliament do that? Should parliament assume the role of an arbitrator in a compulsory arbitration? We have put unions under trusteeship and said we will dissolve the trusteeship when certain conditions are corrected. We can do all these things. But unless our labour laws are changed parliament
(The Chairman.]
will continue to be involved in labour settlements. Frankly, I do not think those kinds of settlements satisfy employers, employees, or the requirements of the nation. We need something better. If we ask workers-and this applies equally to Post Office workers and others in the public sector who are now negotiating-to give up certain rights, should we not bend over backwards to see that they are fairly treated? Is that not how we should treat workers whose work is essential for the national economy and public good?
Without question, the worst employer in Canada is the government. It has never learned how to negotiate with employees. For example, consider the recent public utterances of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien). Given what he said, how can government negotiators negotiate in good faith? Before they can offer an extra cent an hour they must consult the minister or a government representative. Or the cabinet may meet and then it instructs the negotiator to offer an extra one or two cents. Such procedure is totally unreasonable. Negotiators ought to deal eyeball to eyeball; one of them should not need to run to the minister for instructions. Such procedure is unsatisfactory. It hampers government negotiators. If we are to see quick settlement we must change the system.
I remember negotiating with the gold mining industry years ago. You negotiated with a manager and he would say, "Yes, I think we can go so far; will you excuse me." He would leave the room and telephone the board of directors in New York or elsewhere and ask if he could raise the company offer by a certain amount. You negotiated with the man on the other side of the table. In the public service, you do not. You do not negotiate with the man sitting across the table; actually you are negotiating, however indirectly, with the cabinet.

subtopic: WEST COAST PORTS OPERATIONS ACT, 1975 MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING OPERATIONS ON THE WEST COAST

Mr. Speaker, the settlement made in the public service the other day was made on the strength of the longshoremen's settlement. I think my remarks are relevant, as they highlight the need for a new negotiating
system.
Passing this bill will not solve anything. We need to negotiate a new way, a better way. I expect that the negotiator will consider the memorandum of agreement already submitted and then make an award. I hope the men will accept it and go back to work. Nevertheless, if we are to avoid future trouble we must change the law, change the way we handle labour relations in this country, especially in areas where the public interest is paramount. We should introduce a new system which will satisfy better both the employer and employee.
The federal government does not employ competent negotiators. True, one or two are competent, but the majority, particularly in the Department of Labour, are not. We need better arbitrators and conciliators to work in areas which involve the public interest. We should not allow negotiations to deteriorate to the point at which men go on strike. If ordinary negotiations break down the government should supply competent mediation services. At present it employs people in this role who have not been able to do anything else. Most of them are in that
March 24, 1975

category. I admit that one or two public service mediators are competent but the majority are not.
Government mediators need proper training and exposure in various mediation fields. Some provincial mediation and negotiation services are better than federal services. I suggest that passage of this bill will not resolve the problem. If hon. members think it will, they will be disillusioned. For the sake of members of parliament and the general well-being of the country, I hope both the workers and employers will come to terms. That, really, is the purpose of this bill. Nevertheless, we must do things differently in future. When necessary we must give the parties competent help, particularly when the public interest is involved. Let us provide assistance which will lead to mutually acceptable agreements. Nothing less will do. After all we are asking both sides to make sacrifices for the sake of the public good and national reputation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes to make a couple of points which I do not believe have been made today, but have been made on several occasions in the last decade. They concern the matter of ports and, more particularly, grain movement.
It has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and two of his predecessors that the longshoremen have offered to have grain excluded in the handling of cargo during labour disputes in the port of Vancouver. I believe this could apply to a number of other ports as well. Grain could be excluded in a similar way as coal at Robert's Bank is excluded. I am sure the Minister of Labour knows the longshoremen have made this offer several times. They are prepared to work for one employer, whether it be the Canadian Wheat Board, the Board of Grain Commissioners, or the National Harbours Board, although maybe I should not dredge that up.

speechtext:
They are prepared to accept fundamental changes in the system under which they have been working. How many lessons does the government have to learn? We have been through tie-ups caused by grainhan-dlers, weighers and samplers, as well as railroad strikes and walkouts. I do not know how many times these have occurred over the past eight or ten years.
A proposal has been put forward by the longshoremen on at least three or four occasions. The difficulty we have been faced with on each of these occasions could have been dealt with more adequately and more satisfactorily for the farmers, the general public, and those who work handling grain.
Far be it from me or the Minister of Labour to interfere in the internal workings of the different unions. However, I would not be surprised if there was a willingness on the part of the grainhandlers, weighers, samplers and longshoremen to join forces, if not in one union at least in one bargaining unit. This is an area where the Minister of Labour could provide some leadership and encouragement. The Minister of Labour and the government could assist the parties in putting an end to at least this part of the
Longshoremen's Strike
difficulties we are faced with in connection with the movement of grain.
We have been having difficulties in industrial peace in Vancouver harbour, let alone other harbours, which occur in different ways and to different degrees. The leadership has come from some of the workers on several occasions. It has never been followed up by the government or the employers. I want to know why. To be completely cynical, the union has its little group, the employers have their little group, and whenever there is a strike situation the government moves in with ad hoc legislation. If we have to do this six or eight times a decade, obviously that is not good enough.
After our six or seven experiences in the past ten years, I hope the Minister of Labour will sit down with the longshoremen, the grainhandlers, weighers, railroaders and employers' association. The longshoremen have repeatedly said that grain should be removed from general cargo. The issues of automation, and who will handle, fill, unload and load what containers are entirely separate from bulk cargo. They are not even related except for the fact that they occur in the same geographical location.
I do not understand why the government did not get the message years ago. The longshoremen faced up to this a long time ago. They made a proposal that was never taken up. I cannot understand why. If it had been followed up, we would not be in this mess today. I wish to advise the minister and his colleagues that they will get assistance from members on all sides of the House if they do follow it up.
There is a willingness on all sides in Vancouver harbour, and in most other places in the country, to make some fundamental changes with regard to the way the work is performed, who performs it, under what jurisdiction, and who is the employer. Members of parliament might deal with this once every year or so when there happens to be a strike, but these people are on the job every day. They know whereof they speak. Why has this not been grasped by the minister, or by his predecessor who was supposed to be a big wheel in the labour ranks? He never acted on it.
The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and the Farmers Union looked at this offer made by the longshoremen. Nothing happened. Now we meet again to legislate people back to work, denying them a fundamental right.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) pointed out this afternoon that nobody likes to strike. The first person to get hurt by a strike is the one who goes out on one. This parliament and this government have not yet looked at what causes strikes. Proposals have been made by those who handle grain. There is a willingness to make some fundamental changes, but these have not been followed up. If they are not considered after this fracas, I will lose what little faith I have in the abilities and intentions of the Minister of Labour.
I wanted to make these remarks on third reading of this legislation so that I will not have to do this in a year from now when we are dealing with the grainhandlers, weighers, samplers, railroaders or longshoremen. If the minister wants an independent inquiry, a joint group of employees, employers in government or any other mechanism, the

March 24, 1975
Longshoremen's Strike
avenues are there. They have been there for years, but they have not been followed up.
An inquiry into grainhandling has been set up. Are we always going to have ad hoc legislation that flies in the face of what members from all parties in this House desire? These pieces of legislation deal with the matter with great reluctance. They do not get at the root causes of these disputes and strikes. Unless this or any other government deals with the root causes of strikes, people will continue to do things they do not want to do. They will feel they have no other choice. They will feel that no one is listening, and no one is trying to bring them together.
The people on both sides of the quarrel are decent, yet we keep compounding the felony. We let it proceed year in and year out. We still use outmoded concepts and methods. This government always attacks in the wrong way, at the wrong time, and for the wrong reasons. Liberals have a majority; they have an opportunity; they have had it before, but they will not use it.
The Minister of Labour and his officials in his department should sit down with those concerned in Vancouver Harbour, Prince Rupert, Thunder Bay or anywhere else. It makes for good sense and for industrial peace to treat those involved in the movement of bulk commodities differently from those involved in the movement of containers or passenger ships in and out of our seaports. People who work there have been suggesting this for years. I repeat the question: why has nothing happened? Surely some assistance could come in this area from the Minister of Labour and his colleagues.

speechtext: I intend to make one brief comment, Mr. Speaker. I would draw attention to the fact that Bill C-12, which disposed of the grain handling strike and lock-out, contained no provisions for enforcement procedures, whereas the bill now before us does. It seems to me that a precedent has been set-a departure from the practice followed in the other bills, and it has been duly noted. Here, for the first time, to the best of my knowledge, we are being asked to approve of an enforcement procedure. Perhaps the minister, in the course of any statement he might make, would tell the House what has happened in this regard.

speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that a communication has been received which is as follows:
Government House Ottawa, March 24, 1975
Sir,
I have the honour to inform you that the Honourable R. G. B. Dickson, Puisne Judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, in his capacity as Deputy Governor General, will proceed to the Senate Chamber

March 24, 1975

today, the 24th March, at 11.30 p.m. for the purpose of giving Royal Assent to certain bills.
Royal Assent

And being returned:
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant Andre Garneau Brigadier General Administrative Secretary to the Governor General
A message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the House went up to the Senate chamber.
Mr. Speaker informed the House that the Deputy Governor General had been pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent to the following bills:
Bill C-56, An Act to provide for the resumption and continuation of longshoring and related operations at ports on the west coast of Canada.-Chapter No. 32.
Bill C-29, An Act respecting Canadian business corporations.-Chapter No. 33.
Bill C-10, An Act to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act.-Chapter No. 34.
Bill C-373, An Act to provide for the recognition of the Beaver (Castor canadensis) as a symbol of the sovereignty of Canada.-Chapter No. 35.
